While data centers dominate AI workloads due to superior compute density and efficiency, they face scaling constraints: years-long construction timelines, massive capital requirements, and energy grid limitations. L10: History suggests an alternative path forward. From 1946-2009, computing efficiency (performance-per-watt) doubled every 1.5 years (Koomey et al.), enabling a redistribution of computing workloads from data center mainframes to personal computers (PCs). Critically, this transition didn't occur because PCs surpassed mainframes in raw performance: efficiency improvements enabled computing capable of meeting end-user needs within the power constraints of personal devices. L11: We are at a similar inflection point. Local language models (LMs), with ≤20B active parameters, are cite1†surprisingly capable†arxiv.org , and local accelerators (e.g., M4 Max with 128GB unified memory) run LMs at cite1†interactive latencies†arxiv.org . Just as compute efficiency defined the transition to personal computing, we propose that intelligence efficiency defines the transition to local inference. To this end, we introduce intelligence per watt (IPW): task accuracy per unit of power. L12: IPW is a unified metric for measuring intelligence efficiency, capturing both the intelligence delivered (capabilities) and power required (efficiency). L13: We evaluate the current state and trajectory of local inference efficiency through two questions: (1) Are local LMs capable of accurately servicing a meaningful portion of today’s workloads? and (2) Given local power budgets, how efficiently do local accelerators convert watts into intelligence? We conduct a large-scale study across real-world single-turn chat and reasoning tasks, revealing: L14: * Local LMs are capable and improving rapidly: Local LMs can accurately respond to 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries, with accuracy improving 3.1× from 2023-2025. L15: * Local accelerator efficiency has room for improvement: Inference on a local accelerator (Qwen3-32B on an M4 Max) demonstrates 1.5x lower intelligence-per-watt vs. inference of the same local LM on an enterprise grade accelerator (i.e., NVIDIA B200). L16: * Local intelligence efficiency is improving 5.3x from 2023 to 2025: 3.1x from model improvements (thanks to advances in model architectures, pretraining, post-training, and distillation) and 1.7x from accelerator improvements. L17: Call to Action: As AI demand grows exponentially, we must find better approaches to turn energy into intelligence. We envision a world where intelligence is everywhere and in every device: in earbuds providing instant translation, in glasses offering real-time visual assistance, and in pocket assistants solving graduate-level problems. L66: cite12†Image Figure #4: Rapid Improvement of Local LMs across Chat and Reasoning Queries cite13†Image Figure #5: Local LMs approach Frontier Cloud LM Performances. When considering the best-of-local ensemble (routing to the best local model for each query), and the best-of-cloud baseline (routing to the best frontier model), we see that local inference outperforms cloud inference on 3/4 tasks. For our Cloud LMs, we consider Gemini 2.5 Pro (the current SOTA LM on LMArena), Claude 4.5 Sonnet, and GPT-5. L67: Our study reveals three key findings: L68: 1. Local LMs are capable and improving rapidly: Local LMs accurately respond to 88.7% of the collected single-turn chat and reasoning queries with accuracy improving 3.1× from 2023-2025. When considering the best-of-local ensemble (routing to the best local model for each query), local routing surpasses cloud routing on three of four benchmarks (see Figure 4). L69: 2. Local accelerator efficiency has room for improvement: Local IPW can be improved by at least 1.5x to match enterprise-grade accelerators. We benchmarked IPW of Qwen3-32B across 5 enterprise accelerators (2023-2025) and found that inference on the M4 Max (local) achieved 1.5x lower IPW compared to the B200 (enterprise), revealing significant efficiency headroom in local accelerators. L70: 3. Local Intelligence efficiency is improving 5.3x over two years: IPW is improving at 2.3x year-over-year, driven by 3.1x from model innovations (better architecture, pretraining, post-training, and distillation techniques) and 1.7x from hardware advances (see Figure 5). L71: cite14†Image Figure #6: Increase in Intelligence per Watt for Local LMs and Accelerators: Accuracy per watt has improved over 5.3x in two years by selecting the optimal local LM-accelerator pair at each time point. Improvements are driven by advances in both model architectures (from Mixtral-8x7B to gpt-oss-120b) and accelerator hardware (NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 to Apple M4 Max). Evaluated on chat queries and reasoning queries. L72: These findings demonstrate that just as computing shifted from time-shared mainframes to personal computers, LLM inference can shift from centralized clouds to local devices—with smaller, efficient models handling a growing share of queries. Prioritizing IPW in both model design and hardware acceleration will expand the frontier of viable local inference. L73: ## ✅ Limitations and Future Work L74: L75: Our study is a first step towards understanding the viability of offloading portions of frontier LM traffic to local compute. We see several important directions for future work: L76: * Task Coverage: Our study focuses on mainstream chat and reasoning queries. It does not yet include complex or specialized workloads such as long-horizon agentic tasks (e.g., tool use, web navigation) or enterprise use cases (i.e., customer support management). Future iterations will expand the study to account for a full range of LLM deployment scenarios including tasks such as Snorkel Finance and Snorkel Underwriting. L77: * Hardware Diversity: While we profile a large subset of hardware backends, we aim to extend support to a broader range of local accelerators — including more NPUs, desktop laptops (Nvidia DGX Spark), and cell phones. L78: * Intelligence Efficiency in the Cloud: Our work focuses on local inference efficiency. A natural extension is measuring intelligence-per-watt for cloud-scale deployments. L79: * Systems-Level Inference Optimizations: We evaluate the local model and accelerator as integrated components in a single-query setting. Future work will expand IPW to isolate the contribution of individual sub-components of models and accelerators respectively on intelligence efficiency: L80: * Local LM —> Architecture, Pretraining, Post-training, Distillation, etc. L81: * Local Accelerator —> Systems Architecture, Inference Kernels, Quantization Efficiency, Attention Variations, etc. L82: ## 🚀 Towards Intelligence Efficiency L83: We're witnessing a fundamental shift from centralized "mainframe era" inference to distributed "PC era" inference. Local LMs running on local accelerators can accurately answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries—a meaningful subset of total LLM workloads. Intelligence efficiency has improved by 5.3x over the past two years, with local LMs achieving 3.1× accuracy gains and local accelerator efficiency improving 1.7× with substantial headroom for optimization. L84: The path forward is clear: intelligence per watt should be one of the north star metrics for both model architecture and hardware accelerator design. Just as performance-per-watt guided the mainframe-to-PC transition, intelligence-per-watt will guide AI's transition to the edge—expanding the frontier of queries we can redistribute from data centers to local devices. L85: To accelerate this transition, we release a hardware-agnostic profiling harness (Nvidia, AMD, Apple Silicon) for measuring intelligence efficiency across model-accelerator configurations. By establishing a standardized measurement framework, developers can systematically optimize models and hardware vendors can hill-climb on intelligence efficiency rather than raw performance alone. L86: * If you are a hardware developer: we’d love to collaborate in extending our profiling harness to support your new hardware accelerators! L87: * If you are a model developer: we’d love to study your new models and understand whether they improve intelligence-per-watt locally! L14: cite21†View PDF cite22†HTML (experimental) L15: > Abstract:Large language model (LLM) queries are predominantly processed by frontier models in centralized cloud infrastructure. Demand growth strains this paradigm faster than providers can scale. Two advances create an opportunity to rethink it: small, local LMs (<=20B active parameters) now achieve competitive performance to frontier models on many tasks, and local accelerators (e.g., Apple M4 Max) can host these models at interactive latencies.
L16: This raises the question: can local inference viably redistribute demand from centralized infrastructure? This requires measuring both whether local LMs can accurately answer real-world queries and whether they can do so efficiently on power-constrained devices (e.g., laptops). We propose intelligence per watt (IPW), task accuracy per unit of power, as a unified metric for the capability and efficiency of local inference across model-accelerator configurations.
L17: We evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art local LMs, 8 hardware accelerators (local and cloud), and 1M real-world single-turn chat and reasoning queries. For each query, we measure accuracy (local LM win rate against frontier models), energy, latency, and power. We find three key results. First, local LMs successfully answer 88.7% of these queries, with accuracy varying by domain.
L18: Second, longitudinal analysis from 2023-2025 shows IPW improved 5.3x, driven by both algorithmic and accelerator advances, with locally-serviceable query coverage rising from 23.2% to 71.3%. Third, local accelerators achieve at least 1.4x lower IPW than cloud accelerators running identical models, revealing significant headroom for local accelerator optimization.
L19: These findings demonstrate that local inference can meaningfully redistribute demand from centralized infrastructure for a substantial subset of queries, with IPW serving as the critical metric for tracking this transition.
